title: What we have touched (1 John 1:1–4)
hook: the elder writes of what he has seen, heard and touched

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of James, and your line was pray for one another. Did you send that message to someone who's sick? Day six hundred eighty-one.

You can read a whole biography of someone. Dates, places, letters, photographs. And still not know the feel of their handshake, or how their voice sounded saying a name. Some knowing goes through the eyes and ears, and some goes through the skin. Today a new letter opens, called First John. It has no greeting, no name, no to-whom. It starts mid-breath, like a witness on the stand who can't wait to say what he knows. And the first thing he talks about is touch.

In the King James Bible: "That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled, of the Word of life." Listen to the senses pile up. Heard. Seen. Looked upon, a word for gazing, taking it in. And then, handled. Touched. The word means to feel for something, the way you might reach out in the dark. From the beginning echoes the first line of John's Gospel: in the beginning was the Word. For this writer, the Word of life is someone you could touch. Who's writing? The letter never says. Tradition says John the apostle, and the style is close to John's Gospel. Some scholars think it comes from a community shaped by that Gospel, and hear the same voice as the one who calls himself the elder in Second and Third John. Either way, the voice speaks as a witness: we were there, we saw, we touched. And why does he say it this way? Because some people, it seems, were teaching that Jesus only seemed to have a real body. A spirit wearing a costume. The writer answers with his own hands. We touched him, he says. He was real flesh. Then the purpose: "That which we have seen and heard declare we unto you, that ye also may have fellowship with us." Fellowship is a deep word: sharing, partnership, a common life. Not a club. And then the last line of the opening, the reason he's writing at all: "And these things write we unto you, that your joy may be full." He doesn't write to win an argument. He writes so the joy can be full.

Here's the practice: touch something real and give thanks. Settle, and breathe. Put your hand on something near you. The table. Your own arm. A cup. The floor under your feet. Feel it fully: the temperature, the texture, the weight. Notice that you don't have to believe it's there. You know it through your hand. Stay with that for a while. Then, slowly, let your mind move to one person whose hand you've held, and remember the feel of it. If you pray, you can give thanks for what is real and near. The bell holds the time.
Fellowship. First John's reason for writing at all, a deep word for sharing, partnership, a common life: so that your joy may be full.
Your line: joy made full. Today, give one real hug, handshake or hand on a shoulder to someone you love, and let it last a second longer than usual. Day six hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Some churches read 1 John 1:1–4 in the Christmas season, as a witness that the Word became flesh, and use the letter's opening when teaching about fellowship.

original.note: Greek: to touch, handle, feel for something, as in the dark. used in 1 John 1:1.

trapdoor: what you thought: a poetic opening.
what it means: a witness insisting on the senses, heard, seen, touched, so that readers share the fellowship and the joy.
what a scholar hears: psēlaphaō, to handle, and an opening that answers those who said Jesus only seemed to have a body, a view later called Docetism.

notes: The index hook says 'the elder writes'; 1 John itself does not name 'the elder' (2 and 3 John do). The script says 'a teacher later letters call the elder'. Confirm.
Authorship: tradition (Irenaeus and others) attributes the letter to John the apostle; many scholars posit a Johannine community. Both given, unranked.
The opponents' view (Jesus only seemed to have a body, later 'Docetism') is a common scholarly reconstruction; the script hedges with 'it seems'. Confirm.
Use of 1 John 1 in the Christmas season: e.g. readings for the feast of St John (Dec 27) in some calendars. Confirm howItsDone.
